new_statements.quote: Mamaindê stress is first of all conditioned by morphology. When the Mamaindê word is looked at as an unanalyzable sequence, stress is impossible to predict. [...] Mamaindê presents a quantity sensitive stress system, in which stress is assigned to every heavy syllable in the root. Primary stress is on the rightmost of the heavy syllables. In cases where there are no heavy syllables within the root, and quantity cannot play its stress-attracting role, primary stress is still right-headed, being located on the right-most light syllable. [...] The final morpheme classes, those that mark person, tense, and mood, never receive any stress at all, even when they are heavy.
new_statements.citation: Eberhard, David M. 2009. Mamaindê Grammar: A Northern Nambikwara language and its cultural context. PhD dissertation, Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam. Utrecht: LOT (LOT 236).
new_statements.locator: sec. 2.3.4 'Mamaindê Stress: A Prose Description', pp.144-145

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress is confined to the root (stem + stem-auxiliary suffixes): every heavy (closed or long/diphthongal) root syllable is stressed and primary stress falls on the rightmost heavy syllable of the root; if the root has no heavy syllable, primary stress falls on the root-final (rightmost) syllable, whose vowel then lengthens. Because Mamaindê is heavily suffixing with few prefixes, words usually look left-headed at the surface.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on the other heavy syllables of the root and on heavy syllables of the affix classes closest to the root (auxiliary affixes, noun classifiers); outermost person/tense/mood suffixes are never stressed even when heavy; the emphatic /-jeʔ/ carries inherent (lexical) stress (p. ~175).
new_statements.exceptions: Some diphthongs in particular morphological positions fail to attract stress (fn. to 2.3.5); reduplication: stress assigned after the reduplicant is attached and is not. inherent stress on emphatic /-jeʔ/; heavy syllables in outer strata unstressed.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level primary stress computed over the morphological root/stem domain (lexical, stratal); correlates are duration, vowel quality and amplitude, explicitly not pitch (p.141); Mamaindê also has lexical tone (2 tones) independent of stress.
new_statements.identity_note: nort3251 is a Glottolog Bookkeeping languoid for the RETIRED ISO code [mbg] 'Northern Nambikuára', split by CR 2007-017 (effective 2008) into Mamaindê [wmd]=mama1278, Latundê [ltn]=latu1238, Lakondê [lkd]=lako1248, Tawandê [xtw], Yalakalore [xyl], Alapmunte [apv]. The quoted statement describes Mamaindê (mama1278, Guaporé-river cluster; Eberhard treats Negarotê as a closely related separate lect). Mamaindê is ALREADY in the catalog (synchro/tropics/webcat/, source Eberhard 2009 LOT 236), and Latundê/Lakondê/Tawandê are separate check targets. Under the code-currency rule a retired code does not make a separate language: do NOT create a catalog entity for nort3251; nothing new to add beyond the existing mama1278 entry.

sources.quote: Mamaindê stress is first of all conditioned by morphology. When the Mamaindê word is looked at as an unanalyzable sequence, stress is impossible to predict. [...] Mamaindê presents a quantity sensitive stress system, in which stress is assigned to every heavy syllable in the root. Primary stress is on the rightmost of the heavy syllables. In cases where there are no heavy syllables within the root, and quantity cannot play its stress-attracting role, primary stress is still right-headed, being located on the right-most light syllable. sources.locator: sec. 2.3.4 'Mamaindê Stress: A Prose Description', pp.144-145
sources.note: Sec. 2.3.1-2.3.5 (pp.140-160+): stress is 'first of all conditioned by morphology'; within the root it is quantity-sensitive, every heavy root syllable stressed, primary stress on the rightmost heavy syllable of the root, else on the rightmost light syllable of the root; outer affixes (person/tense/mood) never stressed; correlates are length, vowel quality, amplitude, not pitch (p.141).

sources.note: Quadro 71 pp.307-308 and pp.312-313: second-hand summary of Telles 2002 for Latundê/Lakondê (Northern): mixed accent system, partly predictable; domain root and word; in roots the heavy syllable is stressed, two light syllables -> rightmost; primary stress is in the root in Latundê, Lakondê, Mamaindê and Negarotê; in Latundê/Lakondê the leftmost accent is primary, others secondary.
